'''Thomas Brennock Day''' (March 7, 1932{{spnd}}June 15, 2021) was an American scientist and university administrator. He served as the president of [[San Diego State University]] (SDSU) from 1978 to 1996.

==Early life==
Day was born in [[New York City]] on March 7, 1932.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/ws/index.php?pid=38695|title=Nomination of Thomas B. Day To Be a Member of the National Science Board|publisher=The White House|date=May 28, 1985}}</ref>  He was the youngest of six children of an insurance salesman and department store clerk.  His father died when Day was three years old.<ref name="SDUT obit">{{cite news|title=Thomas Day, former SDSU president, dies at 89|url=https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/obituaries/story/2021-06-16/thomas-day-sdsu-dies|first=John|last=Wilkens|date=June 16, 2021|access-date=June 16, 2021|newspaper=The San Diego Union-Tribune}}</ref>  His interest in mathematics and science was piqued after reading [[science fiction]] and listening to stories from his older brother, an engineer who was employed on railroad bridges and tunnels.<ref name="SDSU obit">{{cite news|title=SDSU President Emeritus Thomas B. Day, 1932–2021|url=https://newscenter.sdsu.edu/sdsu_newscenter/news_story.aspx?sid=78462|date=June 16, 2021|access-date=June 16, 2021|publisher=San Diego State University}}</ref>  Day later attended Catholic boarding schools and was awarded a scholarship to attend college.  He studied at the [[University of Notre Dame]] on the recommendation of his mother,<ref name="SDUT obit"/> graduating with a [[Bachelor of Science]] in Physics in 1952.  He went on to obtain a [[Doctor of Philosophy]] in Physics from [[Cornell University]] in 1957.<ref name="SDSU obit"/>

==Career==
Day first worked as a research assistant and later a professor in the physics department at the [[University of Maryland]] in College Park, specializing in theoretical and experimental physics. In 1970, Day became the Vice Chancellor for Academic Planning and Policy at the College Park campus and was later appointed the Vice Chancellor for Academic Affairs at the Baltimore campus.<ref name="SDSU obit"/>  Eight years later, he was appointed the sixth president of [[San Diego State University|SDSU]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://library.sdsu.edu/scua/sdsu-oral-histories/day|title=San Diego State University Oral Histories|work=sdsu.edu}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ccst.us/ccstinfo/fellows/bios/day.php |title=California Council On Science & Technology Fellow Thomas B. Day|work=sdsu.edu}}</ref>

During his tenure, Day was credited with turning SDSU into a major public [[research university]] on par with the [[University of California]] system by increasing grants and research awards.  He was also responsible for expanding the campus infrastructure of SDSU, inaugurating a [[North County (San Diego area)|North County]] campus in [[Vista, California|Vista]] – the precursor of [[California State University San Marcos]] – and helping to establish the present-day [[Graduate School of Public Health, San Diego State University|School of Public Health]] and the School of Communication.<ref name="SDUT obit"/><ref name="SDSU obit"/>  He advocated for [[Affirmative action in the United States|affirmative action]] programs and selected [[Mary Alice Hill]] in 1983 to be the first female [[athletic director]] at a university with a [[Division I-A]] football program.<ref name="SDUT obit"/>  Facing budget shortfalls in 1992, Day proposed sharp cuts that would have eliminated whole departments and laid off faculty.  In August 1992, faculty passed a vote of no confidence in Day and asked the [[California State University Board of Trustees]] to replace him.<ref>"San Diego State Chief Loses Faculty Vote", ''Los Angeles Times'', August 28, 1992</ref> An improvement in the budget situation led to the cuts being rescinded, but Day remained unpopular on campus, and was ultimately asked to resign, ostensibly for health reasons.<ref>"Embattled President of San Diego State to Step Down in '96", ''Los Angeles Times'', February 2, 1995</ref>

Day was a member of the [[National Science Board]] from 1984 to 1996 and a vice-chairman from 1990 to 1994.<ref>[https://www.nsf.gov/nsb/members/former.jsp list of former chairs and vice-chairs on NSF website]</ref>  He was also a Senior Fellow of the [[California Council on Science and Technology]] and a former board member.<ref>[http://ccst.us/ccstinfo/fellows/bios/day.php CCST bio of Day]</ref>

==Personal life==
Day married Anne Kohlbrenner (June 19, 1930 – March 9, 2013) in 1953.<ref name=SDUT-WifeObit>{{cite news |last1=Ogul |first1=Jeremy |title=Anne Day, 82, supported husband's SDSU presidency with charm |url=https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/obituaries/sdut-sdsu-president-wife-dead-2013mar13-story.html |access-date=June 18, 2021 |work=San Diego Union-Tribune |date=March 13, 2013}}</ref>  They met at a party while attending Notre Dame.  Together, they had nine children.  They remained married for 60 years until 2013,<ref name="SDUT obit"/><ref>[http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/utsandiego/obituary.aspx?n=anne-day-kohlbrenner&pid=163662113 Anne Day's obituary]</ref> when she died at the age of 82 due to complications from renal failure.<ref name=SDUT-WifeObit/>

Day died on the evening of June 15, 2021, at an assisted living center in [[Rancho Bernardo, San Diego]].  He was 89 years old.<ref name="SDUT obit"/>
